title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage remains a major cause of brain injury in preterm infants, particularly those born at or before 32 weeks of gestation or with very low birth weight. Hemorrhage originates from the fragile germinal matrix vasculature and may extend into the ventricles and surrounding brain parenchyma, leading to severe intraventricular hemorrhage and periventricular hemorrhagic infarction. Despite advances in perinatal and neonatal care, intraventricular hemorrhage continues to contribute to mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment through mechanisms such as inflammation, white matter injury, posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation, and hydrocephalus. This course reviews the early identification, prevention strategies, and careful postnatal management of periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage that remain central to reducing secondary brain injury.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity discusses the pathophysiology, risk factors, classification, diagnosis, prevention, and management of periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage. Participants will also gain an understanding of factors that identify infants as high-risk, evidence-based screening and preventive practices, cranial ultrasound findings, and complications of this condition. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach to manage this condition, thereby optimizing short- and long-term outcomes in vulnerable neonatal populations.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Introduction
content: Periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage is a major cause of brain injury that affects preterm infants, particularly those born before 32 0/7 weeks of gestation or with very low birth weight. Hemorrhage occurs when vessels of the germinal matrix in the periventricular area rupture, which can then extend into the ventricles as intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH). In severe cases, bleeding will occupy a significant portion of the ventricle and extend into the intraparenchymal area. [1] [2]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Introduction
content: Despite advancements in perinatal care, IVH still contributes significantly to infant morbidity and mortality, as well as long-term poor neurodevelopmental outcomes. IVH is one of the leading causes of death in preterm newborns, although its incidence has decreased. The higher survival rates of extremely preterm infants have resulted in a larger number of survivors with this condition. The initial bleed also causes downstream damage by mechanisms, eg, inflammation, posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation (PHVD), and white matter injury. [3] [4] [5] [6] [7]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Introduction
content: IVH was first discovered by Abraham Towbin in 1968. [8] In 1978, Papile et al developed a classification for periventricular hemorrhage based on head computed tomographic (CT) scans. [9] This classification was later adapted in 1984 for ultrasound, as the equipment is portable and can be frequently repeated. [10] The degree of hemorrhage is graded according to the following categories: Grade I: hemorrhage limited to the germinal matrix Grade II: IVH occupying <50% of the ventricular area without ventricular dilatation Grade III: IVH with ventricular dilatation occupying >50% of the ventricle Periventricular hemorrhagic infarction (PVHI): previously referred to as  Grade IV, IVH with intraparenchymal hemorrhage Grade III and PVHI are often referred to as “severe IVH”.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Etiology
content: The predominant etiology of periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage is the fragility of vessels in the germinal matrix and the immature cerebral autoregulation in preterm neonates.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Etiology
content: Blood vessel morphology in the germinal matrix of the neonate differs from that in other cortical areas, mainly due to the increased metabolic demand required by the rapid turnover of precursor cells in this region. Blood vessels supplying the germinal matrix have a higher density and area than other cortical areas. In addition, the vessel morphology differs, mainly in that vessels supplying the germinal matrix are more rounded than flat in other cortical regions and have incomplete basement membrane development, making them vulnerable to rupture during fluctuations in cerebral blood flow. [11] [2] [12]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Etiology
content: Damage to the surrounding white matter tissue from periventricular hemorrhage has been attributed to compression from ventricular dilation and direct white matter tissue trauma from the weakened ependymal lining. Compression on the adjacent white matter from dilated ventricles has been shown in nonhuman models to produce axonal damage, white matter edema, and various reactive cellular components. A similar mechanism is present when the ependymal lining stretches and ruptures, exposing blood products and other reactive cellular components directly to the white matter. [13] Neonatal transport following outside delivery is the primary risk factor. Neonatal factors include mechanical ventilation, hypercarbia, pneumothorax, respiratory distress syndrome, and frequent intubations. Fluctuation of blood pressure has also shown to be associated with IVH. [14]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Epidemiology
content: The worldwide incidence of periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage ranges from 3.70% to 44.68%. [6] A recent study reported an overall incidence of 36.2%, with severe cases, defined as grade III or PVHI, accounting for 7.1% of infants. [16] The distribution of periventricular hemorrhage by grade in preterm infants shows 17.0% for grade I, 12.1% for grade II, 3.3% for grade III, and 3.8% for PVHI. [16] Approximately 50% of periventricular hemorrhage cases develop within the first day of life, increasing to 90% by the third day. [17]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Epidemiology
content: Since the 1980s, the incidence of periventricular hemorrhage has declined. In Brazil, rates dropped from 50.9% in 1991 to 11.9% in 2005, while the rate of preterm births in the United States has remained stable at 10% in recent years. [6] Periventricular hemorrhage incidence inversely correlates with gestational age and birth weight, with the highest rates among infants born before 28 weeks of gestation. [18] Each additional week of gestation for infants weighing 1000 g or less reduces the likelihood of severe periventricular hemorrhage by 19%, with a 3.5% decrease in incidence for each additional week up to 32 weeks. [19] [20] [19] Overall, IVH incidence among neonates born between 22 and 28 weeks ranges from 16% to 32%. [20] [21]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Epidemiology
content: Weight also influences risk: periventricular hemorrhage occurs in 25% to 30% of neonates weighing less than 1500 g and in up to 45% of those weighing less than 1000 g. [6] Most infants with grade III or PVHI weigh under 1000 g or are born between 22 and 27 weeks of gestation. Severe periventricular hemorrhage occurs rarely (2.7%) in infants with gestational age greater than 31 weeks or weight above 1500 g. [17]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Pathophysiology
content: The germinal matrix consists of an immature, thin-walled capillary network located at the head of the caudate nucleus beneath the ventricular ependyma. [12] [22] This structure develops in fetuses between 24 and 32 weeks of gestation and contains a highly vascular collection of glial and neuronal precursor cells. The germinal matrix encircles the lateral ventricle, with greater prominence at the head of the caudate nucleus. Periventricular hemorrhage arises from the rupture of capillaries in the germinal matrix due to vascular fragility, fluctuations in cerebral blood flow, or coagulation abnormalities. [12] [16] Severe hemorrhage compromises the fragile ependymal layer, allowing bleeding to extend into the ventricles or adjacent intraparenchymal regions. [12]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Pathophysiology
content: Spontaneous rupture of germinal matrix vessels can occur from hypoxia induced by fluctuations in cerebral blood flow. [12] [23] Hemorrhage risk is highest in premature infants during the first 48 to 72 hours of life. Structural immaturity contributes to vulnerability, with defective endothelial tight junctions, basement membrane, pericytes, fibronectin, and astrocyte end-feet. [12] The basal lamina parenchyma remains soft and fragile due to deficient fibronectin and collagen. Preterm intracranial vasculature mirrors the immaturity of other organ systems, increasing susceptibility to rupture. Cross-sectional vessel area reaches its maximum in the germinal matrix, while decreased glial fibrillary acidic protein expression likely weakens the cytoskeleton. Variants of subependymal veins contribute to brittleness and a tendency for thrombosis. High vascular density amplifies fragility, particularly under hypoxic conditions, and the immature vasculature lacks autoregulatory capacity to maintain lumen stability during fluctuating hemodynamics. [12] [24]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Pathophysiology -- Periventricular Hemorrhagic Infarction
content: PVHI has historically been mischaracterized as an extension of IVH due to PVHI often occurring in association with and on the same side as a large IVH and identified following IVH events. Current evidence suggests PVHI develops when IVH obstructs terminal veins, resulting in periventricular venous congestion and hemorrhagic venous infarction. [25] [26] The most common outcome of PVHI is the formation of a large porencephalic cyst. [27]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- History and Physical
content: In the majority of patients, periventricular hemorrhage is found incidentally during ultrasound screening for low-weight or preterm infants. Those with symptoms may show clinical neurological deterioration, respiratory distress, apnea, bulging fontanelle, seizures, hypoactivity, decreased responsiveness, or stupor. Historical features that will predispose an infant to periventricular hemorrhage primarily result from the course of the pregnancy of the mother, including: Gestational age ≤32 weeks The absence of antenatal steroids Antenatal maternal hemorrhage Maternal chorioamnionitis Vaginal delivery [12] [19] [28] [29] [30] [31] The following specific clinical details from the birth of the infant may also increase the likelihood of periventricular hemorrhage in the preterm infant:

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- History and Physical
content: Preterm infants with grade IV periventricular hemorrhage weighed less at birth and had lower gestational ages compared with those diagnosed with grade III. [19] [30] Commonly cited risk factors for periventricular hemorrhage, eg, hypotension, early-onset sepsis, patent ductus arteriosus, surfactant therapy, prenatal steroid administration, maternal bleeding, maternal fever, mode of delivery, Apgar scores, and premature rupture of membranes, do not influence whether an infant develops grade III or grade IV hemorrhage. [30] Both grade III and grade IV hemorrhages occur more frequently in infants born following placental abruption.

content: Antenatal administration of corticosteroids and delivery by cesarean section have each demonstrated a protective effect, reducing the overall incidence of periventricular hemorrhage in preterm infants. [31]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Evaluation
content: The majority of IVH in preterm infants occurs within the first 3 days of life. [32] [33] Of these, 70% of the IVH occurs within the first 24 hours after birth, and 95% occurred within 7 days of life. [34] The diagnosis of periventricular hemorrhage is made via transcranial ultrasound screening. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) currently supports the following guidelines for ultrasonographic IVH screening: All infants born at ≤30 weeks of gestation should be screened by 7 to 10 days of age. Repeat screening is recommended at 4 to 6 weeks of age and at 36 weeks of gestation, or before hospital discharge. Frequent serial cranial ultrasonography is recommended for infants with abnormal findings on cranial ultrasonography. CT scan is not recommended for screening for IVH. Routine magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) before discharge is also not recommended. [1]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Evaluation
content: Although not routinely employed in the initial evaluation, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been demonstrated to be useful in identifying cerebellar hemorrhages and white matter injury. MRI is used to investigate suspected cerebral anomalies found on ultrasound. [35] However, fetal MRI does not add value to standard ultrasound or neurosonography (axial, coronal, and sagittal) for the fetus at risk. [36] Doppler ultrasound and near-infrared spectroscopy monitoring have also been explored as adjuncts to evaluate cerebral blood flow patterns and resistive indices, and abnormal Doppler patterns have been shown to be associated with the development of IVH. [11] Additionally, daily measurement of head circumference is useful to monitor the development of hydrocephalus.Lumbar puncture is not routinely performed as part of the evaluation of IVH. If performed for other reasons (eg, evaluation of sepsis), CSF findings suggestive of IVH include xanthochromia, a high red blood cell count, and a high cerebrospinal fluid protein concentration.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Treatment / Management -- Preventative Strategies
content: The primary treatment strategy for periventricular hemorrhage and IVH should be aimed at the prevention of preterm birth, if possible. This should include the routine administration of antenatal corticosteroids if preterm birth is expected and the transfer of the mother to a facility that has advanced capabilities of caring for very low birth weight infants before delivery. Maternal corticosteroid administration for fetal lung maturation showed a protective effect against periventricular hemorrhage in preterm newborns. [28] In the delivery of the preterm infant, delayed cord clamping should be the routine practice. This method is supported by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and a delay of 30 to 180 seconds has been shown to reduce the risk of periventricular hemorrhage compared with the immediate clamping group. [2]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Treatment / Management -- Preventative Strategies
content: Postnatal management is primarily supportive and focused on minimizing secondary brain injury. Attempts should be made to limit hypoxia and fluctuations in cerebral blood flow and blood pressure. These interventions include head position along the midline, adequate respiratory support, avoidance of physical therapy maneuvers, maintenance of constant blood pressure, and interventions to minimize pain. These interventions should be used at least for the first 72 hours of life, when periventricular hemorrhage has the highest incidence. [17] Multiple care bundles and quality improvement projects have shown promising results using some of the following management recommendations:

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Treatment / Management -- Preventative Strategies
content: Keep the infant in a supine position and the head along the midline (improper positioning may affect jugular venous return). Do not perform physical therapy maneuvers (can cause changes in intracranial pressure and cerebral blood flow). Orotracheal tube suctioning only if necessary (can alter blood pressure, cerebral blood flow, and intracranial pressure). Do not collect cerebrospinal fluid (lumbar puncture will alter heart rate and oxygen saturation). Do not weigh the infant (manipulation can trigger changes in the heart rate, oxygen saturation, and blood pressure). Avoid rapid fluid administration. Delayed cord clamping. Limit skin-to-skin care to every 6 hours. [37] [17] [38]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Treatment / Management -- Preventative Strategies
content: Several pharmacologic agents, eg, phenobarbital and indomethacin, have been studied for the prevention of IVH. The meta-analysis of 10 trials showed a reduction in the incidence of severe IVH with prophylactic indomethacin. [39]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Treatment / Management -- Supportive Therapies
content: Once periventricular hemorrhage has developed, no specific intervention exists to halt the progression of bleeding. Management primarily involves supportive therapies to address associated complications that may develop. Prompt recognition and management of seizures remain critical to prevent additional cerebral injury. Severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, or coagulopathy may require correction in select cases; however, prophylactic transfusions are generally discouraged in the absence of active bleeding. Furthermore, complications, eg, PHVD and hydrocephalus, demand close monitoring and may necessitate surgical intervention depending on severity and clinical presentation.

Furthermore, complications, eg, PHVD and hydrocephalus, demand close monitoring and may necessitate surgical intervention depending on severity and clinical presentation.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis for suspected periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage in preterm infants includes conditions that can present with acute neurologic or systemic instability. These include: Neonatal sepsis (may cause apnea, hypotension, and altered mental status); please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Neonatal Sepsis ," for further information. Metabolic disturbances, eg, hypoglycemia or electrolyte abnormalities Neonatal seizures from nonhemorrhagic causes Meningitis

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis and mortality are directly related to the extent of the injury, gestational age, and associated complications, eg, PHVD. The mortality rate for severe IVH is reported as high as 40%. Any degree of periventricular hemorrhage predisposes to later neurocognitive developments, with rates of cerebral palsy for grades I, II, III, and PVHI at 8%, 11%, 19%, and 50%, respectively. [2] [20] [40] Long-term follow-up and early intervention are recommended for all infants with IVH. [41]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Complications
content: One of the primary complications following periventricular hemorrhage is posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation (PHVD), which can lead to hydrocephalus. Hydrocephalus may be a communicating or noncommunicating type that occurs as a result of impaired cerebrospinal fluid reabsorption or obstruction of the foramen of Monroe.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Complications
content: PHVD should be suspected in any preterm infant with IVH that presents with rapidly increasing head circumference. Clinically, infants should be monitored by daily head circumference measurement and examination of the anterior fontanelle. Hydrocephalus can be monitored by measuring either the Evans ratio (the ratio of bifrontal horn diameter to the biparietal bone diameter) or the frontal and occipital horn ratio (FOHR), which is the average of the frontal and occipital horn dimensions divided by the biparietal diameter. [42] [43] Although both measurements can exhibit interobserver variation, serial measurements on ultrasound are more meaningful.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Complications
content: Another commonly used measurement tool is the “ventricular index”, which is assessed by cranial ultrasound in the coronal view. The ventricular index is the distance between the midline (falx) and the lateral border of the lateral ventricle at the level of the foramen of Monro. [44] Neurosurgical consultation is required when the FOHR is greater than 0.55 or the ventricular index exceeds the 97th percentile, and significant clinical findings, eg, split sutures, bulging fontanel, and bradycardia, are present. [45] Multiple treatment strategies have been proposed for hydrocephalus, including serial CSF drainage, subgaleal shunt placement, ventricular reservoir placement, or ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement. [2] [29] A lack of consensus remains among neonatologists, pediatric neurologists, and pediatric neurosurgeons as to the best management of PHVD. [42]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Complications
content: Periventricular leukomalacia is an ischemic white matter injury, frequently diagnosed by ultrasound or MRI. IVH may contribute to the development of periventricular leukomalacia. A correlation between impaired cognitive function and periventricular leukomalacia in infants has been observed. Production of free radicals following IVH, ischemic insult after large IVH, and release of iron from ventricular blood contribute to white matter injury and the occurrence of periventricular leukomalacia. Although not specific, a cranial ultrasound performed before discharge or at 36 weeks postmenstrual age is important for screening for periventricular leukomalacia. Periventricular leukomalacia may be the primary cause of neurodevelopmental delay following periventricular hemorrhage. [29]

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Effective deterrence of periventricular hemorrhage and IVH in preterm infants relies on both prenatal and postnatal strategies aimed at minimizing risk factors and supporting fragile neonatal vasculature. Prenatal interventions include the routine administration of antenatal corticosteroids when preterm birth is anticipated, which promotes fetal lung maturation and reduces hemorrhage risk. Cesarean delivery may further decrease the incidence in select high-risk pregnancies. During delivery and the early neonatal period, delayed cord clamping, careful handling to avoid rapid fluctuations in cerebral blood flow, midline head positioning, and minimization of invasive procedures, eg, unnecessary suctioning or lumbar puncture, help limit additional stress on the fragile germinal matrix. Continuous monitoring of blood pressure, oxygenation, and acid-base status during the first 72 hours of life—when the majority of periventricular hemorrhage cases occur—remains essential for preventing progression and secondary injury.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education for families focuses on promoting understanding of the condition, its risk factors, and the rationale for preventive interventions. Parents of preterm infants should receive counseling on the importance of antenatal care, including steroid administration and early hospital transfer to facilities equipped for very low birth weight infants. Education also emphasizes the necessity of gentle handling, adherence to monitoring protocols, and recognition of early warning signs, eg, apnea, lethargy, seizures, or bulging fontanelles. By combining evidence-based deterrence measures with family-centered education, healthcare teams can enhance vigilance, improve adherence to preventive strategies, and support optimal short- and long-term outcomes for vulnerable neonates.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage is a common and serious form of brain injury in preterm infants, particularly those born before 32 weeks’ gestation or with very low birth weight. It results from the fragility of the germinal matrix vasculature combined with immature cerebral autoregulation, making the neonatal brain vulnerable to fluctuations in cerebral blood flow during the early postnatal period. IVH ranges from mild hemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix to severe forms associated with ventricular dilatation or periventricular hemorrhagic infarction. While advances in perinatal care have reduced overall incidence, IVH remains a major contributor to neonatal mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment, largely due to secondary complications such as posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation and white matter injury.

title: Periventricular and Intraventricular Hemorrhage -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective management of periventricular and intraventricular hemorrhage requires coordinated interprofessional care focused on prevention, early detection, and mitigation of secondary injury. Physicians, including neonatologists and pediatricians, are responsible for risk stratification, stabilization of cerebral hemodynamics, interpretation of neuroimaging, and longitudinal prognostication. General practitioners and advanced practitioners contribute by ensuring continuity of care, monitoring growth and development, and facilitating timely referrals for neurodevelopmental follow-up. Nurses play a critical role in bedside surveillance, minimizing handling, maintaining optimal positioning, and promptly identifying clinical changes that may signal complications. Pharmacists support safe medication use, including vasoactive agents, analgesia, and seizure management, while helping reduce iatrogenic risk. Close communication among team members, shared decision-making with families, and coordinated transitions from the NICU to outpatient care are essential to enhance patient safety, optimize outcomes, and deliver family-centered, high-quality neonatal care.
